about.title: Walnut Creek Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Walnut Creek is home to roughly 68,910 residents, and on any given afternoon far more people pass through its shops, offices, and restaurants along N Main Street and Treat Boulevard. Every one of those properties has an owner or manager responsible for keeping walkways, entrances, and parking areas reasonably safe. When a fall happens, the question under California law is usually notice: did the owner know about the hazard, or should they have discovered it, and did they fail to fix it or warn you? That is where evidence matters most. A photo of the spill before it was mopped, the name of the employee who saw you fall, and a written request that the business preserve its camera footage can decide a case months later. Time also works against you. Most premises claims in California must be filed within two years, and a claim against a public entity, such as a city sidewalk or a county building, carries a much shorter window. LawProactive is a free service, not a law firm. Tell us what happened, and we will connect you with an independent Walnut Creek attorney who works on contingency, meaning no fee unless there is a recovery.

whyChoose.title: How a Walnut Creek Premises Liability Attorney Can Help

items.title: Building the notice case
items.desc: California requires proof that the owner knew or should have known about the hazard. An attorney gathers maintenance logs, inspection schedules, and prior complaints to show how long the condition existed.

items.title: Preserving surveillance before it disappears
items.desc: Many Walnut Creek stores and parking structures record over their footage within days. A prompt preservation letter from an attorney is often the only way that video survives.

items.title: Protecting your claim under comparative fault
items.desc: California applies pure comparative fault, so a property owner may argue you were partly to blame. Your attorney pushes back on that argument and manages the two-year deadline, or the shorter one for public entities.

items.question: I fell in a store parking lot off Ygnacio Valley Road. Who is responsible, the store or the landlord?
items.answer: It depends on who controlled that area under the lease and who handled maintenance. Sometimes the tenant, the property owner, and a separate management company each share responsibility. An attorney can request the lease and maintenance contracts to sort out who owed you a duty of care.

items.question: The manager said the spill had only been there a minute. Does that end my claim?
items.answer: Not by itself. Notice can be shown through inspection records, how the hazard formed, and whether employees were nearby, not just the manager's estimate. Surveillance video is often the clearest way to establish how long the condition existed, which is why preserving it quickly matters.

items.question: What if I tripped on a city sidewalk or in a public building in Walnut Creek?
items.answer: Claims against a public entity in California follow a much shorter timeline than the standard two years, and you generally must file a formal government claim first. Missing that window can bar the case entirely. Reach out early so an attorney can confirm which deadline applies to your situation.
